prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and opened new tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest discovery-or-invention case on the shortlist. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift and recoil/Doppler problems in one conceptual step, and Ye's work turned it into an instrument with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, enabling clock comparisons, tests of constants and relativistic geodesy. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by many independent laboratories and the interpretation is stable. A two-name prize is compact and the 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (ion control) prizes are precursors, not duplicates. It also gathers the broadest opening support, with four first places and six top-three rankings, though I do not treat support as merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap. Lattice-clock credit is shared with Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and others who are not in the credited names, and the single-ion and comb lineages (Hall, Haensch, Wineland) already received prizes, so the citation must be worded carefully to avoid appearing to re-reward them. The practical payoff, a redefinition of the SI second, has not happened yet, and one could argue an instrument achievement is less of a physics discovery than a conceptual advance such as topological band theory.

responses.point: Pearce ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, as a theory prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald followed by the decisive correlated-insulator and superconductivity experiments of Jarillo-Herrero, and finds the maturity adequate after roughly eight years.
responses.response: I agree that the field is broad and the theory-plus-experiment pairing is attractive, and I ranked it sixth rather than nowhere. But I would qualify the maturity argument. The nature of the superconducting pairing and of many correlated states is still debated, and the experimental credit is split with Cao, Dean, Young and Kim-type groups that the three credited names do not cover. Clock accuracy, by contrast, is measured and compared across continents, which is a harder form of confirmation. I would keep twisted bilayer graphene as a strong later candidate rather than the first prize.

responses.point: Johansson puts circuit QED first as the architecture of nearly every superconducting processor, but flags the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits as a timing concern and discloses connections to that community.
responses.response: I take the timing concern seriously and think it counts against B005 now: a second superconducting-circuit prize within a year after Clarke, Devoret and Martinis risks looking repetitive, and the credit boundary with the transmon is unclear. I also note that quantum error correction, which Johansson ranks third, rests on experiments that are still early, as he says himself. I would treat B005 as a candidate for a later year rather than this one, and I welcome his disclosure of a connection as a reason for his view to be weighed with care.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory first as the most consequential theory-to-materials advance, ranks optical lattice clocks only eighth, and accepts that the credited trio is defensible but not complete because of Metzner, Rozenberg and others.
responses.response: I share the respect for DMFT; I ranked it fifth, and it is a framework used daily. But a method prize is harder to anchor to one discovery, and the exclusion of Metzner, who co-founded the infinite-dimension limit, makes the three-name allocation visibly incomplete. I also do not accept that clocks are a lesser achievement for being an instrument. Optical lattice clocks have a sharp concept, a measurable result and independent validation, and they fall squarely under invention of lasting benefit to physics. I would like to hear which finite-dimensional failures Eriksson considers disqualifying.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first as the most unambiguous discovery, fully mature and overdue, while accepting that the credited names stand in for thousands of collaborators.
responses.response: The scientific importance is not in doubt, and I would agree the 2013 prize left the experimental side unrecognised. My difficulty is the same one he names: a prize to Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee honours detector leadership as a proxy for two collaborations, and does not include the accelerator builders or analysis coordinators. That leaves the citation open to the charge of arbitrariness in a way the two-person lattice-clock prize is not. I would accept it as a serious alternative only if the committee can state a principled attribution rule, which I cannot yet do.

uncertainties: Whether the citation should name or acknowledge other lattice-clock groups (Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke) and the ion-clock lineage, which I cannot verify beyond background knowledge.
Whether the pending but not yet decided redefinition of the SI second matters for timing, or whether the demonstrated 1e-18 performance is already sufficient.
Whether the committee prefers a conceptual discovery (topological insulators, B030) to an instrument achievement when the support is this close.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My work in active matter, turbulence and random matrices is not on this shortlist, and I know of no documented personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the other credited names.
